gaps.sentence: There are plenty ___ chairs for everyone.
gaps.hint: 'plenty' is always followed by this preposition before a noun
gaps.explanation: 'Plenty of + noun' is the fixed pattern; no other preposition follows 'plenty'.

gaps.sentence: I don't like this colour — do you have it in ___ colours?
gaps.explanation: 'Other colours' uses 'other' as an adjective before the plural noun; 'another' is followed by singular nouns.

gaps.sentence: ___ of the milk has gone off, so do not drink it.
gaps.explanation: 'All of the milk' — 'whole' would need 'the whole of the milk'.

gaps.sentence: She gave the children two sweets ___.
gaps.hint: distribution per child at the end of the sentence
gaps.explanation: 'Two sweets each' means two per child; 'every' cannot stand alone here.

gaps.sentence: We can take the ferry or the tunnel — ___ way takes about three hours.
gaps.hint: one of two options, singular noun
gaps.explanation: 'Either way' means whichever of the two you choose; 'both' would need 'ways'.

gaps.sentence: ___ John and his brother are doctors.
gaps.explanation: 'Both John and his brother are ...' links two people affirmatively; 'neither' and 'either' pair with 'nor/or'.

gaps.sentence: It's so quiet here — there's hardly ___ around.
gaps.explanation: 'Hardly' is a negative adverb, so it combines with 'anybody' (hardly anybody = almost nobody); 'nobody' would double the negative.

gaps.sentence: He took ___ notice of the warning and carried on as before.
gaps.explanation: 'Take little notice of' means to pay hardly any attention; 'notice' is uncountable here.
